title: Choroidal Folds: Clinical Masterclass & Diagnostic Algorithmic Approach
summary: Choroidal folds represent undulations of the RPE-Bruch membrane-choriocapillaris complex, often mimicking disc edema. This guide provides a comprehensive clinical framework for differentiating mechanical from infiltrative causes of choroidal buckling.

sections.title: Definition & Pathophysiology
sections.content: Choroidal folds (striate choroidopathy) involve physical buckling of the inner choroid and RPE. Pathophysiology is usually mechanical (hypotony, posterior scleritis) or infiltrative (tumors, inflammation). The folds typically appear as alternating light and dark lines, often horizontal in the posterior pole.

content.explanation: H: Hypotony (Post-surgical), I: Inflammation (Scleritis), S: Scleral buckling/masses, T: Tumors (Choroidal hemangioma/melanoma), O: Orbital processes (Pseudotumor), R: Retinochoroidal scarring, R: Retrobulbar mass, Y: Young patients (Idiopathic).

sections.title: Red Flags: When to Worry
content: Proptosis or eyelid fullness (suggests Orbital Mass)

sections.title: Diagnostic Workup Algorithm
content: 1. Slit-lamp biomicroscopy (+90D) to identify alternating striae.
4. CT Orbit/MRI (If orbital mass is suspected).
5. FA/ICGA (To rule out choroidal neovascularization or inflammatory activity).

sections.title: Clinical Pearls for the Boards
content: Choroidal folds usually preserve vision unless they involve the fovea.
They are commonly mistaken for papilledema; however, the vessel caliber in choroidal folds is usually normal.
Fluorescein Angiography reveals alternating hyper/hypofluorescent lines corresponding to the peaks and valleys of the folds.
If associated with disc edema, prioritize ruling out posterior scleritis and orbital masses first.
